terms.definition: A poetic device where successive lines, pairs of lines, or stanzas begin with consecutive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. Found in Psalm 119 and Lamentations 1-4, this structure aided memorization in oral cultures.

A figure of speech where clauses are related through reversal of their structure in an inverted parallel pattern (A-B-C-B'-A'). The central element (C) often contains the main point. Named after the Greek letter chi (χ).
terms.example: Whoever sheds man's blood, by man his blood shall be shed (Genesis 9:6)

terms.definition: A text that builds progressively to a high point, with each element increasing in force or meaning, often moving from lesser to greater or from physical to spiritual realities.

A long narrative, often in elevated style, combining many episodes. The Exodus account (Exodus through Deuteronomy) functions as a biblical epic, though uniquely focused on God's acts rather than human exploits.
Beginning and ending a passage with similar or identical phrases to mark boundaries and emphasize themes.
terms.example: Psalm 8 begins and ends with 'O LORD, our Lord, how majestic is your name in all the earth!'

terms.definition: Building progression where each line increases in force or meaning, creating a sense of mounting importance or urgency.
The hallmark of Hebrew poetry, where lines echo, contrast, or build upon each other

subtypes.description: The second line restates the first in different words
The second line contrasts with the first
The second line builds upon or completes the first

terms.definition: Regular repetition of a line or phrase in poetry to mark sections.
terms.example: The repeated phrase in Psalm 136, 'His love endures forever'

terms.definition: A narrative or argument that circles back to its beginning, often on a larger scale than chiasm, creating a sense of completeness.
Recurring narrative patterns used to convey familiar situations.
terms.examples: Betrothal stories at wells (Genesis 24, 29; Exodus 2) or annunciation narratives

terms.definition: An extended metaphor where elements systematically correspond to other meanings. The entire narrative operates on both literal and symbolic levels.
Repetition of the same initial sounds of adjacent or nearby words, used for narrative effect. Often only visible in the original Hebrew, Aramaic, or Greek.
An indirect reference to something understood from personal or cultural context.
terms.example: John 8:58, 'Before Abraham was, I AM' alludes to Exodus 3:14

terms.definition: Attribution of human bodily characteristics to God (hands, eyes, feet, walking). Helps finite humans understand an infinite God. Distinguished from theophany (actual divine appearance in human form).
Attribution of human emotions or passions to God (anger, joy, regret, jealousy). A subset of anthropomorphism focusing specifically on feelings and psychological states.
Repetition of the same internal sounds of adjacent or nearby words, used for narrative effect. Primarily recognizable in original languages.
Indirect expression for something considered indelicate or sensitive.
terms.examples: 'knew his wife' for sexual relations, 'uncovered nakedness,' 'feet' as euphemism for genitals

terms.definition: Intentional exaggeration for emphasis or rhetorical effect.
terms.examples: 'If your right eye causes you to sin, pluck it out' (Matthew 5:29), 'easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle' (Matthew 19:24)

terms.definition: An implied comparison without using 'like' or 'as' and without explicitly stating both elements being compared. More subtle than direct metaphor.
An expression whose meaning differs from its literal words, unique to a particular language and culture.
terms.examples: 'kick against the goads,' 'gird up your loins,' 'heap coals of fire'

terms.definition: Saying one thing but meaning another, often for dramatic effect.
terms.example: Elijah mocking the prophets of Baal, 'Perhaps he is sleeping' (1 Kings 18:27)

terms.definition: Deliberate understatement for effect, often using negative construction.
terms.example: Paul calling himself 'not inferior to the most eminent apostles' (2 Corinthians 11:5)

terms.definition: Expressing totality by naming opposite extremes or polar pairs.
terms.examples: 'heaven and earth' = universe (Genesis 1:1), 'evening and morning' = whole day, 'searched me and known me, sitting down and rising up' = all activities (Psalm 139)

terms.definition: Direct comparison without 'like' or 'as'.
terms.examples: 'The LORD is my shepherd' (Psalms 23:1), 'You are the salt of the earth' (Matthew 5:13)

terms.definition: Substituting an associated term for the thing meant. A trope of association where one term stands for another typically broader term.
terms.examples: 'the crown' for the king, 'the sword' for war, 'blood' for death or life, 'Red Sea' evoking the exodus event

terms.definition: Short narrative with a spiritual or moral lesson, often using everyday situations to illustrate deeper truths. May serve as illustrations but not standalone doctrine.
Giving human qualities to non-human things.
terms.examples: 'Wisdom calls out in the streets' (Proverbs 1:20), 'Let the mountains sing' (Psalms 98:8)

terms.definition: Short, memorable saying expressing general truth or wisdom, characteristic of wisdom literature.
Comparison using 'like' or 'as'.
terms.example: 'He will be like a tree planted by streams of water' (Psalms 1:3)

terms.definition: Objects or actions representing deeper realities (bread and wine, lamb, water, light and darkness). The physical represents spiritual truth.
A subcategory of metonymy using a part to represent the whole or vice versa.
terms.examples: 'all flesh' = all people, 'daily bread' = all food, 'give us this day our daily bread' includes all necessities
terms.note: Also called 'eponymy' when an individual stands for a nation (Jacob for Israel)

terms.definition: A person, event, or thing in the Old Testament that prefigures another in the New Testament.
terms.example: The bronze serpent (Numbers 21:9) as a type of the Cross (John 3:14-15)

terms.definition: Directly addressing absent persons, abstract concepts, or inanimate objects.
terms.examples: 'O death, where is your sting?' (1 Corinthians 15:55), 'O Jerusalem, Jerusalem' (Matthew 23:37)

terms.definition: 'Blessed is/are...' statements expressing divine favor. Prominent in Jesus' Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5:3-11).
Making an inference based on an already established lesser reality to prove a greater one.
terms.example: 'If God so clothes the grass of the field...will he not much more clothe you?' (Matthew 6:30)

terms.definition: Making an inference from a greater established reality to a lesser one.
Question asked for effect rather than information.
terms.examples: 'How long, O LORD?' (Psalms 13:1), 'Shall we continue in sin?' (Romans 6:1), 'What is man that you are mindful of him?' (Psalms 8:4)

terms.definition: 'Woe to...' statements pronouncing judgment or warning. Common in prophetic literature.
Showing two or more things to be similar, helping readers understand one thing in terms of another.
Showing two or more things to be different from one another, often using 'but' to highlight differences.
Direct speech between characters. In biblical narrative, everything gravitates toward dialogue, which carries the theme forward.
Presenting an idea or event followed by its interpretation, helping readers understand significance.
The perspective from which a narrative is told, revealing the author's intended emphasis and theological message.
Background or setting for events or ideas that will be presented, providing necessary context.
The basic unit of biblical narrative, usually containing no more than two characters or groups functioning as characters. God often appears as one of the characters.
Correspondence addressing specific situations in early churches, containing doctrine, instruction, and pastoral care.
Unique literary form presenting the good news about Jesus Christ. Highly episodic and different from other ancient biographical genres.
Legal codes, commandments, and covenant stipulations governing Israel's relationship with God and community life.
Story-telling that records God's redemptive work. The most common literary form in the Bible, operating on multiple levels from individual stories to the ultimate narrative of God's kingdom.
Speeches and sermons delivered to audiences, recorded in both testaments.
Uses parallelism, imagery, figurative language, and terseness rather than rhyme and meter. Found throughout Scripture, especially in Psalms, Song of Songs, and prophetic literature.
Messages from God delivered through prophets, including judgment oracles, promises of restoration, and visions of the future.
Practical and philosophical reflections on life, righteousness, and the fear of the Lord. Includes Job, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes.
The process of explaining or drawing out the meaning of a text. Critical analysis to determine what the original author intended to communicate.
The science and art of biblical interpretation. The principles and methods used to understand and apply Scripture correctly.
Interpretive approach that seeks the meaning intended by the original author through examining the historical context and grammatical structure.
The normal or customary usage of a word or expression. The plain meaning intended by the author within its genre and context.
Meaning that refers to a concept represented in terms of another, departing from literal usage for rhetorical or theological purposes.
The surrounding text that helps determine how a passage should be interpreted. Includes the verses before and after, the chapter, the book, and the broader biblical narrative.
An appearance of God in visible, often human form. Distinguished from anthropomorphism, which is figurative language. Examples include God's appearance to Abraham (Genesis 18) and Moses (Exodus 3).
A genre of revelatory literature using highly symbolic imagery, visions, and cosmic imagery to reveal divine mysteries about the end times and God's ultimate victory. Found in Daniel and Revelation.
Deliberate use of numbers for symbolic or structural purposes.
terms.examples: 'x, x+1' formula ('three things...four things' in Proverbs 30), groups of seven throughout Scripture

terms.definition: Witty use of word meanings and ambiguities, often visible only in original languages.

A method of preaching in which the main idea, structure, and application of the sermon arise from and are controlled by the biblical text. The text drives the message rather than serving as a springboard for the preacher's own ideas.

A form of expository preaching in which the main points of the sermon are drawn from a single, shorter passage, often a verse or two. The scope of the text is narrow but the handling is exegetically grounded.

A preaching method organized around a topic or theme, drawing from multiple texts. At its best each text is handled exegetically; at its weakest, texts are used as proof-texts for a predetermined conclusion.

The practice of preaching through a biblical book sequentially, passage by passage, over a series of weeks or months. A discipline for ensuring the congregation hears the whole counsel of God rather than only the preacher's favorite themes.
A discrete passage or unit of Scripture selected for reading or preaching, with identifiable beginning and ending markers determined by the flow of the text.

An approach that situates every passage within the overarching story of redemption, tracing how the text relates to God's saving purposes culminating in Christ. Guards against both moralism and proof-texting.

The hermeneutical and homiletical principle that all Scripture ultimately points to, prepares for, or reflects Christ. Contrasted with moralizing application that bypasses the gospel and treats biblical characters as mere examples to imitate.

A three-stage method of Bible study and sermon preparation: what does the text say? (observation), what does it mean? (interpretation), how does it apply? (application). Each stage depends on the one before it.

The conceptual move from the meaning of a text in its original historical and cultural context to its meaning and application for today's audience. Requires identifying the timeless principle beneath the culturally specific form.

The single, unifying statement that captures the sermon's main point in one complete declarative sentence. Typically composed of a subject and complement, the proposition controls the entire message and ensures unity of theme.
The broad topic of a sermon or passage — what the text is generally about. The subject is incomplete on its own and must be narrowed by the complement to form a full proposition.
What the text specifically says about the subject. Together, the subject and complement form the complete proposition of the sermon.
The structural skeleton of a sermon, organizing main points and subpoints in a logical, memorable sequence. May be deductive (proposition stated first) or inductive (proposition delayed or implied).
A major supporting idea that develops or proves the sermon's proposition. Most sermons contain two to five main points, each of which must relate directly to the proposition.
A subordinate idea that develops, explains, or supports a main point. Subpoints provide the detail and texture that make main points persuasive and clear.
A sermon structure in which the proposition is stated at the outset and then developed and defended through the body of the message. The audience knows where the sermon is going from the beginning.

A sermon structure in which the conclusion (proposition) is withheld until the end, building toward it through a series of observations, questions, or narrative movements. Creates suspense and engagement.
A sermon outline in which the points are stated in contemporary language accessible to the audience, as distinct from an exegetical outline that follows the text's own structural language.
An outline that traces the logical or structural movement of the biblical text itself, often serving as an intermediate step before developing the homiletical outline for delivery.
The guiding question used to generate the main points of a sermon (e.g., 'Why?', 'What?', 'How?'). The interrogative ensures unity and logical development throughout the message.
terms.example: A proposition stating 'We should trust God in trials' combined with the interrogative 'Why?' yields main points beginning with reasons.

terms.definition: The question used to develop a single main point within the sermon, as opposed to the interrogative which governs the sermon as a whole. Keeps each individual section focused and internally coherent.
A connecting statement between sermon units (introduction to body, point to point, body to conclusion) that signals movement, summarizes what has been established, and previews what is coming.
A brief restatement of what has been covered at a transition point within the sermon, reinforcing retention and aiding comprehension before moving to the next section.

The opening portion of a sermon designed to gain attention, create need, and orient the audience to the passage and proposition. Should move the listener from where they are to where the text wants to take them.
An opening element — a question, story, striking statement, or tension — designed to capture the audience's attention and draw them into the message before orienting them to the text.
A question posed in the introduction that the sermon will answer, creating a felt need and a sense of direction. Invites the audience into the problem the text addresses.

The closing portion of a sermon, typically summarizing the proposition, driving home the application, and calling for a response. Often the most important moment for retention and life-change; should not introduce new material.

A specific, concrete invitation or charge given at the close of a sermon calling the audience to respond in a particular way — to believe, repent, obey, pray, or act. Should be the natural culmination of the sermon's application.

In classical rhetoric, the conclusion of a speech — typically a summary of the argument and an emotional appeal designed to move the audience to decision. The sermonic conclusion corresponds to the peroration.
Expressing the meaning of a text or sermon point in different words, often simpler or more concrete, to aid comprehension. A tool for ensuring that what was said was actually heard and understood.
Clarifying the precise meaning of a key term, word, or concept in the sermon, often drawing on the original languages, lexicons, or historical context to establish meaning before applying it.
An examination of a key biblical term in its original language, tracing its usage across the biblical corpus and relevant literature to clarify its specific meaning in a given context.

Information about the cultural, historical, geographical, or social setting of a text that illuminates its original meaning and helps the audience understand what the text would have communicated to its first readers.

Examination of the syntactical structure of a text — the function of words, phrases, and clauses — to determine meaning. Includes attention to verb tense and mood, conjunctions, subordinate clauses, and sentence flow.
A story, example, analogy, or image used to make an abstract truth concrete and memorable. Illustrations function as windows that let light into an idea, not ornaments added after the fact.

An explanation of something unfamiliar by comparing it to something familiar. Functions as a bridge between the known and the unknown, enabling the audience to grasp a concept through a parallel they already understand.

A brief, often personal or biographical story used to introduce, reinforce, or conclude a point. Should be tightly connected to the idea being illustrated and not draw more attention to the storyteller than to the truth.
A longer narrative or scenario developed in enough detail to carry sustained explanatory or emotional weight. More powerful than a brief anecdote but requires careful pacing and relevance.
An illustration that shows what a concept is not, clarifying truth by contrast. Helps define the boundaries of an idea by demonstrating its opposite or its distortion.
A concrete, physical object used to illustrate a spiritual or theological truth. Engages sensory attention and makes abstract ideas tangible, particularly effective in teaching contexts.

A story or example drawn from church history, world history, or biography to illuminate a point. Adds credibility and depth, connecting the congregation to the broader story of God's work across time.

The bridge from the meaning of the text to the life of the listener — what the text demands, invites, or promises in concrete, contemporary terms. The 'so what' of preaching. Application should flow from interpretation, not precede it.
The process of moving from a culturally specific biblical command, narrative, or example to the timeless principle it embodies, as a necessary step toward valid contemporary application.

A truth derived from a biblical text that transcends its original historical setting and applies across all cultures and times. The stable theological or moral content beneath the culturally conditioned form.
Application that specifies concrete actions or changes in behavior the listener should make in response to the text. Addresses the question: what should I do differently?

Application that targets internal dispositions, mindsets, or affections — the way one thinks or feels — rather than only external behavior. Addresses the question: what should I believe or value differently?
A direct appeal calling the audience to act on or respond to what has been taught. Often the concluding movement of a sermon, urging the congregation toward obedience, faith, or repentance.

A truth or demand that is not explicitly stated in the text but necessarily follows from what is stated. Good preaching draws out implications without treating them as having the same authority as direct biblical assertions.

The conscious burden, question, or struggle the audience brings to the sermon. Effective preaching addresses felt needs as entry points, then connects them to the deeper diagnosis and remedy the text provides.

Application that specifically addresses the gospel — how the text relates to salvation, justification, sanctification, or the person and work of Christ. Guards against moralistic preaching that demands change without providing the gospel's resources for it.

Intentional consideration of the specific listeners — their knowledge, needs, struggles, level of biblical understanding, and cultural context — in order to pitch the sermon at the right level with the right emphases.

The core proclamation of the gospel, particularly as identified in NT scholarship: the death, burial, resurrection, and Lordship of Christ. Distinct from didache (ongoing teaching/doctrine), though the two are closely related.
terms.example: The apostolic sermons in Acts (2:14–36; 13:16–41) represent the kerygma in its most concentrated form.

terms.definition: Christian teaching or instruction, as distinguished from the initial gospel proclamation (kerygma). Addresses the ethical formation, doctrinal grounding, and discipleship of those who have already received the kerygma.

Moral exhortation or ethical instruction in a biblical text, particularly in the epistles. Identifying paraenetic sections is important for accurate application, as they often assume a doctrinal foundation laid earlier in the letter.

A truth claim that can be stated as a declarative sentence with a definite meaning — either true or false. The backbone of doctrinal and expository preaching, affirming that Scripture communicates objective content, not merely experience.

A rhetorical technique common in Hellenistic philosophy and Paul's letters involving an imaginary dialogue with an interlocutor — raising objections and answering them. Critical for interpreting passages such as Romans 2–3 and 6.
terms.example: 'What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin so that grace may abound? By no means!' (Romans 6:1–2)

terms.definition: The credibility, character, and trustworthiness of the speaker as perceived by the audience. In classical rhetoric, one of the three primary modes of persuasion. A preacher's ethos shapes whether listeners receive the message.

The emotional dimension of communication — the speaker's ability to move, stir, or connect with the audience's feelings. One of Aristotle's three modes of persuasion. Authentic pathos arises from genuine belief in and engagement with the text.

The logical, rational content of the argument — the quality of the reasoning and evidence. One of Aristotle's three modes of persuasion. In preaching, logos corresponds to the careful exegetical and theological substance of the message.

Knowledge of God's existence and attributes attainable through reason and observation of creation, apart from special revelation. Includes cosmological, teleological, and moral arguments for God's existence.

The discipline of gathering and organizing the teachings of Scripture topically — on God, humanity, sin, salvation, the church, and last things — into a coherent, comprehensive, and internally consistent whole.

The discipline that traces the progressive unfolding of God's redemptive plan through the canonical storyline, attending to the historical development of revelation across the Testaments and the literary context of each book.

The study of how the church has interpreted and formulated Christian doctrine across history — councils, creeds, controversies, and theologians — providing context for current theological discussions.
The discipline of defending and commending the Christian faith — answering objections, providing evidence, and demonstrating the reasonableness and truth of Christian truth claims (1 Peter 3:15).

The apologetic method associated with Cornelius Van Til arguing that every system of thought rests on unproven foundational commitments and that Christian theology provides the only coherent foundation for knowledge, logic, and ethics.

The apologetic method that moves in two stages: first establishing theism through natural theology (cosmological, teleological, moral arguments), then establishing Christianity specifically on that theistic foundation.
A doctrinal topic or 'place' in systematic theology — the traditional term for chapters or major divisions in a systematic theology (e.g., the locus on God, on sin, on salvation).
The introductory matters addressed at the beginning of a systematic theology — the nature and task of theology, the sources and norms of authority, and the role of reason and revelation.
Right belief — conformity to the established doctrinal teaching of the historic Christian faith, as measured by Scripture and the ecumenical creeds. Contrasted with heterodoxy and heresy.

Teaching that departs from orthodox doctrine but remains within a broad Christian framework. Less severe than heresy; heterodox positions may still affirm the core of the faith while erring on secondary matters.

A serious doctrinal error that strikes at the essential content of the Christian faith — the Trinity, the person of Christ, the nature of salvation. Heresy places one outside the bounds of Christian orthodoxy.
The error that Christians are under no obligation to observe the moral law, since they are saved by grace alone. Addressed directly by Paul in Romans 6:1–2 and throughout the NT ethical sections.
The error of treating law-keeping as the basis of acceptance before God, or of adding man-made regulations to Scripture as binding conditions of righteousness. Opposed in Galatians and Colossians.

Authoritative gatherings of church representatives that formulated binding doctrinal definitions — Nicaea (325), Constantinople (381), Ephesus (431), and Chalcedon (451) being the four most widely recognized.

Formal summaries of Christian doctrine. Creeds (Apostles', Nicene, Athanasian) are broadly ecumenical; confessions (Westminster, Heidelberg, Belgic, London Baptist) belong to particular Reformed or Baptist traditions.

The approach to speaking about God by what he is not — denying creaturely limitations of God as a way of preserving his transcendence and incomprehensibility. Contrasted with cataphatic (positive) theology.
God's act of making himself and his will known. Divided into general revelation (through creation and conscience) and special revelation (through Scripture and Christ).

God's self-disclosure through creation, conscience, and history, available to all people at all times. Sufficient to leave humanity without excuse before God but not sufficient for saving knowledge of Christ.
God's direct disclosure of himself and his redemptive purposes, given to particular people at particular times, culminating in the written Scripture and the incarnate Christ.

The supernatural work of the Holy Spirit by which God so moved the human authors of Scripture that what they wrote was the Word of God — without overriding their personalities, vocabularies, or historical contexts.
The doctrine that inspiration extends to the very words (verbal) of Scripture in all its parts (plenary), not merely to concepts or ideas. Every word of the original text is God-breathed.
The way God's sovereign action and human authorship work together fully and simultaneously in inspiration — the words are genuinely the human author's and at the same time genuinely God's Word.

The property of Scripture by which it, in its original manuscripts, makes no errors in anything it affirms — whether in matters of theology, history, or the physical world. Distinguished from infallibility by its positive scope.

The property of Scripture by which it unfailingly accomplishes its purpose and does not mislead in matters of faith and practice. Sometimes used synonymously with inerrancy; in other usage, a narrower claim limited to salvific matters.
The original manuscripts of Scripture as produced by the biblical authors. Inerrancy applies strictly to the autographa, not to any translation, copy, or manuscript tradition.
The property by which a book is recognized as belonging to the authoritative collection of Scripture. The canon refers to the closed list of books acknowledged as inspired and binding.
Books included in the Septuagint and the Roman Catholic canon but not in the Hebrew Bible or Protestant Old Testament. The authority of the Apocrypha has been disputed since the early church.

The doctrine that Scripture is sufficiently clear in its central teachings that ordinary believers, using ordinary means of study, can understand what is necessary for salvation and godly living — without requiring an authoritative magisterium.

The doctrine that Scripture contains all that is necessary for salvation, faith, and practice. Nothing essential has been omitted, and no extrabiblical source carries binding authority alongside Scripture.

The principle that God condescends to communicate in ways suited to human understanding and finite capacity. Associated with Calvin, accommodation explains how infinite truth is expressed in finite, culturally embedded human language without error.

Latin for 'the fuller sense.' The idea that the divine author intended a deeper or fuller meaning in a text than the human author was fully aware of — often applied to OT passages fulfilled in the NT.
terms.example: Isaiah 7:14 in its original context and its fulfillment in Matthew 1:23.

terms.definition: The meaning the human author intended to communicate in writing. In evangelical hermeneutics, authorial intent is the locus of a text's meaning and the primary goal of exegesis.
God's self-existence and self-sufficiency — he exists from himself and depends on nothing outside himself for his being. God is the uncaused cause, the only being who exists necessarily.
God's unchangeableness in his being, perfections, purposes, and promises. Distinct from God acting within time and responding within history; immutability concerns his nature, not his activity.

The classical doctrine that God does not undergo involuntary emotional changes or suffer as creatures do. Closely related to immutability and widely debated in modern theology, particularly in relation to the suffering of Christ.
God's unlimited power to do all that is consistent with his nature and will. Omnipotence does not entail the ability to do what is logically self-contradictory or contrary to his character.

God's complete and perfect knowledge of all things — past, present, future, and possible — including the free acts of creatures. God's knowledge is immediate, exhaustive, and not derived from observation.
God's simultaneous presence everywhere in his fullness. Distinct from pantheism; God is present to all creation without being identical with it or contained by it.
God's perfect and infinite goodness and love as a defining attribute of his nature, such that everything God does flows from and is consistent with his essential goodness.
The classical doctrine that God is not composed of parts — his attributes are not additions to his being but are identical with his essence. God does not have love; God is love.

God's relationship to time — either timelessness (existing outside time altogether) or everlastingness (existing through all time without beginning or end). Both views are defended in evangelical theology.
God's existence above, beyond, and independent of creation. He is qualitatively other than and not contained by the universe — the Creator distinct from his creation.
God's active presence within and engagement with creation. Held in tension with transcendence; the biblical God is both infinitely above creation and intimately present within it.
God's nature exceeds full human comprehension. We can know him truly and genuinely through revelation, but we cannot know him exhaustively. Finite minds cannot contain the infinite God.

Divine attributes that God shares in analogous (not identical) form with human beings made in his image — love, wisdom, holiness, justice, knowledge. Creatures possess these attributes derivatively and finitely.
Divine attributes that belong to God alone and are not shared with creatures — aseity, omniscience, omnipotence, omnipresence, eternality, and simplicity.
The belief that there is one and only one God. The foundational commitment of biblical religion over against polytheism (many gods), henotheism (one god among many), and pantheism (all is God).

The Trinity as revealed in the history of redemption — the Father sending the Son, the Son accomplishing redemption, the Spirit applying salvation. The 'economy' refers to God's ordered activity in the world.
The Trinity as God is in himself, apart from the work of creation and redemption. The eternal relations among the persons prior to and independent of creation.
The eternal, non-temporal relation by which the Son is begotten of the Father — not a beginning in time but a defining characteristic of his person within the immanent Trinity.
The eternal relation by which the Spirit proceeds from the Father (and, in Western theology, from the Son — filioque). Defines the Spirit's personal distinction within the Godhead.
The mutual indwelling of the three persons of the Trinity in one another. Affirms the unity of God without collapsing the real distinctions among Father, Son, and Spirit.

Latin for 'and from the Son.' The Western church's addition to the Nicene Creed affirming that the Spirit proceeds from both Father and Son — a major point of division between Western Christianity and Eastern Orthodoxy.

The image of God in which humanity was created (Genesis 1:26–27). Theological debate centers on what constitutes the image — rationality, morality, relationality, representative dominion, or a combination of these.

The state of sinfulness and guilt inherited by all of Adam's natural descendants as a result of Adam's first transgression. Includes both original guilt (liability to punishment) and original corruption (inherited sinful nature).

The doctrine that sin has affected every aspect of human nature — intellect, will, emotions, and body. Not that every person is as sinful as possible, but that no part of humanity is unaffected by the fall.
The doctrine that Adam acted as the legal representative or covenant head of all humanity, so that his sin is justly reckoned to all his descendants. Contrasted with natural headship.

The view that humanity sinned in Adam because all people were physically present in him as their common ancestor, making the imputation of Adam's sin a matter of shared identity rather than representation.
The reckoning or crediting of sin or righteousness to another's account. Adam's sin is imputed to humanity; humanity's sin is imputed to Christ; Christ's righteousness is imputed to the believer.

Disordered desire or inordinate inclination toward sin — the remaining bent toward sin in fallen human nature. Used in Catholic theology particularly for the tendency toward sin that persists even after baptism.
The view that human beings consist of three distinct parts: body, soul, and spirit — the spirit being a higher faculty specifically relating the person to God.
The view that human beings consist of two parts — body and soul/spirit — the spirit and soul referring to the same immaterial aspect of personhood rather than distinct substances.
The view that the soul is transmitted from parents to children along with the body, explaining the inheritance of original sin as a natural transmission rather than a divine creative act.

The view that God creates each individual soul directly at conception or birth. The dominant position in Reformed theology, though it creates some tension with explaining how original sin is transmitted.

The condition of fallen humanity in which the will is genuinely free but completely bound in its orientation — inclined only toward evil and unable to choose God savingly without the transformation of divine grace.
The branch of systematic theology concerning the person and work of Jesus Christ — who he is (his divine and human natures) and what he has accomplished (his atoning and mediatorial work).
The doctrine that in the one person of Jesus Christ two complete natures — divine and human — are united without confusion, change, division, or separation. Defined at the Council of Chalcedon (451).

The communication of attributes — the properties of each of Christ's two natures being truly predicated of his one person. Because of the hypostatic union, both 'the Son of God died' and 'the Son of Man is omniscient' are valid affirmations.

From Philippians 2:7 — Christ 'emptied himself' in the incarnation. Kenotic theories debate what Christ relinquished or veiled; classical theology holds he set aside the independent exercise of certain attributes while retaining them essentially.
The eternal Son of God taking on full and complete human nature — becoming truly and permanently human while remaining truly and fully divine. The Word became flesh (John 1:14).
The miraculous conception of Jesus in the womb of the virgin Mary by the Holy Spirit, without a human father. Fulfills Isaiah 7:14 and is essential to the sinlessness and unique identity of Christ.
Christ's freedom from sin — in act (he never sinned) and in nature (he had no sinful inclination). Whether Christ was peccable (able to sin but did not) or impeccable (unable to sin) is debated.
Christ's perfect fulfillment of the law's positive demands throughout his entire earthly life, credited to the believer as the positive righteousness required for justification before God.

Christ's willing submission to the penalty of the law — his suffering and death — satisfying divine justice on behalf of sinners. Active and passive obedience together constitute his complete atoning work.

The threefold office of Christ: as Prophet he reveals God and his will; as Priest he atones for sin and intercedes; as King he rules and protects his people. A framework developed by Calvin and standard in Reformed theology.
Christ's ongoing work as the risen and ascended High Priest, pleading his completed sacrifice before the Father on behalf of his people — a present and unceasing ministry (Hebrews 7:25; Romans 8:34).
The branch of systematic theology concerning the person and work of the Holy Spirit — his deity, his distinct personhood within the Trinity, and his saving and sanctifying ministry.

The Spirit's work of uniting the believer to Christ and to the body of Christ at conversion (1 Corinthians 12:13). In Pentecostal and charismatic theology, a distinct post-conversion empowering experience accompanied by speaking in tongues.

The Spirit's ongoing work of empowering and directing the believer for service and godliness (Ephesians 5:18). Distinct from the Spirit's permanent indwelling; the filling may vary in intensity and is a repeated experience.
The character qualities produced in the believer by the Spirit's sanctifying work (Galatians 5:22–23): love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, and self-control.

Supernatural capacities given by the Spirit to believers for the building up of the body of Christ. Whether miraculous gifts continue today is the central debate between cessationism and continuationism.

The Spirit's work of opening the minds and hearts of believers to understand and receive the truths of Scripture. Distinct from inspiration, which produced Scripture; illumination enables its comprehension and application.
The Spirit's work of bringing a person to a genuine sense of sin, righteousness, and judgment — the necessary preparation for repentance and saving faith (John 16:8–11).
The Spirit's work of marking believers as God's possession and guaranteeing their eschatological inheritance. The Spirit himself is the seal and the down payment (Ephesians 1:13–14; 4:30).

Latin for 'order of salvation.' The logical (and for some, temporal) sequence of the Spirit's saving work in the individual — typically including effectual calling, regeneration, faith, repentance, justification, adoption, sanctification, and glorification.
God's internal, Spirit-empowered summons that infallibly brings the elect to faith. Distinguished from the general or external call of the gospel which goes to all who hear the message.
The new birth — the Spirit's sovereign work of giving spiritual life to the spiritually dead. In Reformed theology, regeneration logically precedes and enables saving faith rather than following it.
The human side of coming to salvation, comprising repentance (turning from sin) and faith (turning to Christ). Conversion is the conscious response enabled by the prior work of regeneration.

God's forensic declaration that a sinner is righteous — not by infusing righteousness but by imputing Christ's righteousness and forgiving sin on the basis of Christ's atoning work received through faith alone.

The ongoing work of the Holy Spirit transforming the believer progressively in holiness of life. Distinct from justification, which is positional and complete; sanctification is experiential and progressive.
The once-for-all aspect of sanctification by which the believer is set apart from the dominion of sin at the moment of conversion. The basis from which progressive sanctification proceeds.
The final stage of salvation in which the believer's body is resurrected and the entire person is fully conformed to the image of Christ. The completion of the ordo salutis at the return of Christ.
The act by which God, in justification, receives believers as his children and heirs, conferring upon them the rights and standing of sons in his household (Romans 8:14–17; Galatians 4:4–7).

The doctrine that those who are truly regenerate will persist in faith to the end and not finally fall away — grounded in God's electing purpose and preserving grace, not the believer's own strength or willpower.

The believer's confidence that he or she is genuinely saved and will persevere to glory. Debated whether assurance is of the essence of saving faith itself or is a distinct blessing that may be more or less fully possessed.

A genuine turning from sin — involving intellectual acknowledgment of sin, emotional grief over it, and volitional turning away from it toward God. Repentance and faith are inseparable components of conversion.

The satisfaction of God's wrath against sin through Christ's atoning sacrifice, turning away divine judgment. Focuses on the Godward direction of the atonement. Distinguished from expiation, which focuses on sin itself.

The removal or covering of sin's guilt and defilement by Christ's sacrifice. Focuses on sin rather than on God's wrath. Distinguished from propitiation, which concerns the turning away of divine displeasure.
The purchase or liberation of sinners from bondage to sin, Satan, and death by Christ's payment of the ransom price — his own life given as a substitutionary sacrifice.
The restoration of the broken relationship between God and humanity through Christ's atoning work, removing the enmity created by sin and establishing peace between the Creator and the creature.

The doctrine that Christ died in the place of sinners, bearing the penalty they deserved. The broader category under which penal substitution falls, encompassing any view in which Christ acts as a substitute.

The specific atonement theory holding that Christ bore the legal penalty due to sinners — satisfying divine justice — as their substitute. The central atonement model in Reformed and much evangelical theology.

The atonement view associated with Abelard holding that Christ's death primarily serves as a demonstration of God's love intended to move sinners to repentance, without satisfying divine justice or substituting for sinners.

The atonement view holding that Christ's death was not a payment of the exact penalty owed but a public demonstration of God's moral governance, allowing God to forgive on relaxed terms without strict satisfaction.
The atonement motif associated with Gustaf Aulén emphasizing Christ's death and resurrection as a cosmic victory over sin, death, and the devil, liberating captive humanity from their power.
The Calvinist doctrine that Christ's atoning work was designed to secure the salvation of the elect specifically — infinite in worth and sufficient for all, but particular in design and intent.

The view that Christ's atoning work was intended for all humanity without exception, though its saving benefit is received only by those who believe. The position of Arminian and many four-point Calvinist traditions.

In Arminian theology, the grace God extends to all people prior to and enabling their free response to the gospel — removing the effects of total depravity sufficiently to allow genuine, uncoerced choice.

The Calvinist doctrine that God's saving grace, when applied to the elect, infallibly accomplishes its purpose — not by overriding the will but by transforming it so that the sinner willingly and gladly comes to Christ.
The view that regeneration and salvation are the work of God alone — the sinner contributes nothing to the initiation of salvation. The Calvinist and Lutheran position with respect to regeneration.
The view that salvation involves genuine cooperation between divine grace and human free will — God and the sinner work together. The Arminian and Roman Catholic position.
God's non-saving grace extended to all people — restraining sin, enabling civic virtue and cultural achievement, and sustaining creation. Distinct from the special or saving grace given to the elect.
The branch of systematic theology concerning the nature, marks, mission, and government of the church.
The church as God knows it — all the truly regenerate across all times, places, and denominations. Known only to God; not identifiable by human observation.

The church as it appears in the world — the gathered community of those professing faith and their children, including both the regenerate and the unregenerate. The proper sphere of church discipline.

The identifying characteristics of a true church. In Reformation theology: the pure preaching of the Word and the right administration of the sacraments. Some traditions add church discipline as a third mark.
The form of church government. The three main forms are episcopal (governed by bishops), presbyterian (governed by elders), and congregational (governed by the congregation as a whole).

In Catholic and some Protestant traditions, an outward sign instituted by Christ that confers grace to participants. Protestants generally limit sacraments to baptism and the Lord's Supper; many prefer the term 'ordinance.'

The term preferred in Baptist and many evangelical traditions for baptism and the Lord's Supper — emphasizing that they are acts ordained by Christ to be observed, not means that automatically confer grace.

The practice of baptizing infants, grounded in covenant theology's identification of baptism as the NT counterpart to circumcision, applied to children of believers as members of the covenant community.
The practice of baptizing only those who make a credible profession of faith, held by Baptist, Anabaptist, and many evangelical traditions. Baptism follows regeneration and publicly signifies it.
The meal of bread and cup instituted by Christ at the Last Supper and observed by the church in his memory. Theological debates center on the nature of Christ's presence in or with the elements.
The Roman Catholic doctrine that at consecration the substance of the bread and wine is transformed into the actual body and blood of Christ, though the accidents (outward appearance) remain.
The broad term for views holding that Christ is truly and bodily present in the Lord's Supper — used by Lutherans and some Anglicans. Contrasted with memorialism's purely symbolic view.

Calvin's mediating position that Christ's body is in heaven but the Holy Spirit makes the risen Christ truly (though spiritually) present to the faith of the communicant, so that the Supper is a genuine means of grace.
The view that the Lord's Supper is a memorial of Christ's death and a symbol of his body and blood — Christ is present spiritually by faith but not bodily in or with the elements.
The process by which the church addresses sin among its members — from private correction to public excommunication — aimed at the restoration of the sinner and the purity of the community.
An ordained leader of a local church responsible for teaching, governance, and pastoral care. Some traditions distinguish teaching elders (pastors) from ruling elders who govern but do not preach.
A church officer responsible for mercy ministry and practical service, distinct from the elder's governing and teaching role. Rooted in Acts 6 and the qualifications of 1 Timothy 3:8–13.

The view that the miraculous sign gifts — including tongues, prophecy, and healing — ceased with the close of the apostolic age and the completion of the NT canon, having served their purpose of authenticating the apostles.
The view that all spiritual gifts, including miraculous ones such as tongues and prophecy, continue to operate in the church today and were not limited to the apostolic era.
The branch of systematic theology concerned with last things — death, the intermediate state, resurrection, final judgment, and the consummation of God's kingdom.

The tension in NT eschatology between the kingdom of God inaugurated in Christ's first coming (already) and its full consummation awaiting his return (not yet). The framework for understanding the overlap of the ages.

The view that the last days have genuinely begun with Christ's first coming — the kingdom is truly present but awaiting final consummation. Associated with Geerhardus Vos and further developed by Oscar Cullmann.
The view associated with C.H. Dodd that the kingdom of God has been fully realized in Christ's ministry, with little or no future dimension remaining. Contrasted with inaugurated eschatology.
Greek for 'presence' or 'arrival.' The NT term for Christ's second coming in glory to judge the living and the dead and to consummate his kingdom.

The thousand-year reign of Christ referenced in Revelation 20:1–6. Interpreted differently by amillennialists, premillennialists, and postmillennialists, generating one of the major eschatological debates in evangelical theology.

The view that the millennium is not a future literal thousand-year earthly reign but describes the present church age between Christ's first and second comings, during which Christ reigns at the right hand of the Father.

The view that Christ will return before the millennium and reign on earth for a literal thousand years. Divided into historic premillennialism (without the dispensational framework) and dispensational premillennialism.

The form of premillennialism that includes a pre-tribulation rapture, a literal seven-year tribulation, a restored national Israel, and a sharp distinction between God's program for Israel and for the church.
The form of premillennialism that expects Christ's return after a period of tribulation, without the dispensational distinction between Israel and the church or a separate rapture event.

The view that the gospel will progressively transform the world, resulting in a golden age of Christian civilization (the millennium), after which Christ will return. The millennium precedes the second coming.

In dispensational theology, the catching up of living and deceased believers to meet Christ in the air, distinct from and preceding the second coming. Derived from 1 Thessalonians 4:17. Debated as pre-, mid-, or post-tribulational.

The condition of the soul between physical death and the final resurrection. Evangelical theology generally holds to conscious existence — the believer in the presence of Christ, the unbeliever under judgment.

The view that the dead are unconscious between physical death and the final resurrection. Rejected by most evangelical traditions on the basis of passages such as Philippians 1:23 and 2 Corinthians 5:8.

The final reckoning at which all people stand before God to receive the verdict on their lives — the righteous to eternal life, the unrighteous to eternal punishment (Matthew 25:31–46; Revelation 20:11–15).
The traditional evangelical doctrine that the unrighteous suffer consciously and without end in separation from God, receiving the just penalty of their sin against an infinitely holy God.

The view that the unrighteous are ultimately destroyed rather than suffering eternally — they cease to exist after final judgment. Held by some evangelical scholars as a biblical alternative to eternal conscious punishment.

The eschatological renewal of all things — the restoration and transformation of the present creation into the new heavens and new earth, the eternal dwelling place of God with his redeemed people (Revelation 21–22).

A system of biblical interpretation organized around the covenants of works and grace (and sometimes redemption), tracing one unified redemptive plan across both Testaments with continuity between Israel and the church.

In Reformed covenant theology, the pre-fall arrangement between God and Adam in which eternal life was offered on the condition of perfect and personal obedience. Adam's failure necessitated the covenant of grace.

In Reformed covenant theology, God's one redemptive covenant running from the fall to the consummation, administered through successive epochs (Abrahamic, Mosaic, Davidic, New Covenant), all pointing to and fulfilled in Christ.

The eternal intra-Trinitarian covenant in which the Father elects a people, the Son agrees to redeem them through incarnation and atonement, and the Spirit agrees to apply salvation. The eternal basis for the covenant of grace.

A system of biblical interpretation dividing redemptive history into distinct ages (dispensations) under different divine arrangements. Emphasizes a sharp distinction between Israel and the church and a future for national Israel.

A mediating form of dispensationalism that sees more continuity between the Testaments and holds that Christ's present reign at the right hand of the Father partially inaugurates the Davidic kingdom already.

A mediating position between covenant theology and dispensationalism, rejecting the covenant of works and the Mosaic covenant as binding on NT believers, while maintaining the unity of God's redemptive purpose across the Testaments.

The way in which OT persons, institutions, and events prefigure and find their full and intended realization in Christ and the new covenant realities he introduces. Distinct from mere prediction-fulfillment.
